reading.rtitle: The Paragraph That Fits Every School
paras: Every year, admissions readers encounter a paragraph that seems to have been written for no school in particular. It praises a world-class faculty, a vibrant community and a commitment to excellence. It mentions a beautiful campus and a strong program. It is pleasant, grammatical and entirely forgettable, because it could be sent, without changing a word, to several hundred institutions. The paragraph is not dishonest. It is simply addressed to no one.

The Why Us supplement exists precisely to separate that paragraph from its alternative. Colleges ask the question not because they need reassurance about their own quality, but because they want evidence that an applicant has imagined, in some detail, a life inside their particular classrooms. A supplement that repeats the language of the brochure provides no such evidence. Arguably, it suggests the opposite: that the applicant has read the brochure and stopped there.

The alternative requires research, and research of a particular kind. A useful way to organize it is a three-part test. The first part is specificity: a real course, a real person, a real program that exists at this college and, ideally, at few others. The second is connection: a link between that detail and something the applicant has already done, read or wondered about. The third is trajectory: a sense of where that connection might lead over four years. A supplement that passes only the first test reads like a catalog. One that passes only the second reads like a personal essay that has wandered into the wrong form. The strongest supplements pass all three in a few sentences.

Consider a fictional example. An applicant to a small liberal arts college writes that the art history department offers an interdisciplinary course on the chemistry of pigments, taught jointly by an art historian and a chemist. That sentence is specific. The applicant then explains that a lesson on Vermeer left her wondering why a particular blue was once more precious than gold, and what it was actually made of. That is the connection. Finally, she mentions that she would like to pursue conservation science, perhaps through the college museum's summer program. In roughly eighty words, a reader has met someone who could not have written the same paragraph about any other school.

Precision at this level is partly a matter of vocabulary. Colleges describe themselves in carefully chosen terms: a seminar-based first year, object-based teaching, close mentorship. An applicant who uses those terms accurately sounds like someone who has already begun to think inside the institution. The danger lies in borrowing them uncritically. Mirroring a college's language demonstrates research only when each borrowed term is attached to something the applicant actually wants to do. Otherwise it is the brochure again, with better grammar.

There is one final rule, and it is the least glamorous. Every fact must be checked. Courses are renamed, professors move, programs close. A supplement that confidently names a professor who left three years ago tells the reader something about the applicant, though not what the applicant intended. The best writers of these short essays are, in the end, careful researchers first.

gist.prompt: Which statement best summarizes the writer's advice?
choices: A strong supplement lists as many courses and professors as possible to prove research.
A strong supplement links verified, specific details about one college to the applicant's own questions and future path.
A strong supplement praises the college's reputation in the institution's own words.

items: The writer considers the generic paragraph dishonest.
'The paragraph is not dishonest. It is simply addressed to no one.'
According to the writer, colleges ask the question to collect evidence that applicants have imagined life in their classrooms.
They 'want evidence that an applicant has imagined, in some detail, a life inside their particular classrooms'.
The writer believes that specificity alone is enough for a strong supplement.
'A supplement that passes only the first test reads like a catalog.' All three parts are needed.
The writer warns that using a college's own vocabulary can backfire.
'The danger lies in borrowing them uncritically... Otherwise it is the brochure again, with better grammar.'
The writer suggests that naming a professor who has left reveals nothing about the applicant.
It 'tells the reader something about the applicant, though not what the applicant intended'.

items.situation: Lesson 1 recall. Nominalize: "Vermeer refused to decorate the wall, and that is what makes the picture arresting."
tips: Vermeer's refusal to decorate the wall is what makes the picture arresting.
Turn the verb into a noun and make it the subject.

items.situation: Lesson 2 recall. Calibrate: "The painting looks simple but is really complex."
tips: One adverb can carry the whole contrast.

items.situation: Lesson 3 recall. Make it point: "The light calls Matthew, not the gesture."
tips: It is the light, not the gesture, that calls Matthew.

items.situation: Lesson 4 recall. Lift it: "I understood the question only months later."
tips: Only months later did I understand the question.
Restrictive expression first, then auxiliary before subject.

items.situation: Lesson 5 recall. Concede and answer: "The sculptures were safe in London, so they should stay."
tips: Granted, they were safe in London; safety alone does not settle ownership.
Grant the point, then answer it.

items.situation: Today. Fix the collocation: "I want to make research about pigments and I have a big passion about color."
tips: I want to conduct research on pigments, and color has become a genuine fascination.
Conduct research on; a fascination with. And drop passion.

listenings.text: Okay, everyone, if you can gather around the steps for a second. I have given this tour about sixty times, and I can tell you exactly what families ask about. Dorms, food, and whether the gym is open late. Those are fair questions, and I am happy to answer them. But I wish more of you asked what a normal Tuesday in class actually feels like, because that is what you will be doing for four years. Mine looked like this. My first-year seminar had twelve students around one table, and every single week there was an object from the campus collection in the middle of it. A coin, a letter, a small painting. We were not allowed to look anything up until we had spent twenty minutes just describing it. So here is my advice for your Why Us supplement, and I promise it is not in the brochure. Write about something you saw or did on this visit that you could not have read on our website. The admissions office knows what the website says. They wrote it.

Thank you all for coming. Let me tell you what I do not care about when I meet students who are thinking about art history. I do not care whether you already know the names of famous artists, or whether you can list the movements of the twentieth century in order. You will learn those things here, quickly, and frankly they are the easy part. What I look for is harder to fake. I look for students who ask a real question about an object, and who are willing to stay with that question long enough to discover that their first answer was wrong. That willingness is rare, and it is the foundation of everything we do. One more thing, since some of you are writing supplements. Please be careful with the word passion. Everyone uses it, so it tells me nothing at all. I would much rather hear about one object that kept you awake at night, and what you still do not understand about it.
